Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arjun Mehta is a 37-year-old South Asian American psychologist, married, who presented for treatment following a terrorist attack he survived approximately fourteen months ago. He had been attending a professional conference at a hotel in a mid-sized American city when gunmen entered the building and opened fire in the lobby and adjacent corridors. Arjun had been walking toward the elevator bank when the first shots rang out — a sound that seemed, in that initial half-second, almost abstract, almost like something falling. Then the screaming began. He pressed himself behind a luggage cart, unable to move, unable to think, watching a man he had spoken with at breakfast fall to the floor twenty feet away. He lay there for what he later learned was forty-seven minutes before law enforcement cleared the building. He was physically unharmed. He has described that period of waiting as the most total and consuming helplessness he has ever known — not a fleeting feeling but a state that seemed to rewrite something fundamental about how the world worked.

In the weeks that followed, Arjun returned to his practice and his marriage, and for a time he convinced himself that the event was behind him. He was, after all, a clinician who understood trauma. He knew the literature. He had treated patients with PTSD. What he had not anticipated was how thoroughly that knowledge would fail to protect him from his own experience. The nights became the first problem. He began waking in the dark in a state of acute alarm, heart hammering, room unrecognisable for several seconds. He started leaving a lamp on, then the hallway light, then the television running through the night. His wife, Priya, adapted without complaint at first, but months of disrupted sleep have left a quiet strain between them that neither has fully named.

Sounds became a persistent difficulty. A car backfiring in the parking structure beside his office building once sent him to the floor behind his desk — an episode he has not disclosed to any colleague. He works in a suite shared with two other clinicians, and the proximity of a busy street means that sharp, percussive sounds arrive without warning. He has come to dread the walk from his car to the building entrance, scanning the environment in a way that he recognises, intellectually, as hypervigilant, but that he cannot simply decide to stop. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt less like a thought than a physical fact, that the world was genuinely and indiscriminately dangerous — that safety was a story people told themselves before something happened to them.

What frightened him most, in a way that cut deeper than the startle responses or the sleeplessness, was what he saw when he looked at himself. The person who had spent fifteen years helping others articulate and metabolise their suffering now found himself drifting away during sessions — sliding into a kind of internal elsewhere, a diffuse, imagined space where nothing required his attention. He recognised this in himself with a clinician's precision and a patient's shame. He had also begun drinking more than he ever had — a glass of whiskey before bed, then two, then occasionally something in the early evening as well, framed to himself as unwinding, as managing, as what anyone might need. He has been careful about it, he says, though he acknowledges the carefulness itself is a signal worth noting.

Arjun has avoided, wherever possible, situations in which he feels his control over outcomes is uncertain — cancelling a planned flight to visit family, stepping back from a co-facilitated trauma group at a community clinic, declining a conference invitation. Each decision felt reasonable in isolation. Together, over fourteen months, they have narrowed his life considerably. He had come to believe he simply could not prevent bad things from happening, and so the only available response was to reduce exposure to anything that might require him to find out.

What finally brought him to seek help was a session three weeks ago in which a patient described feeling trapped and powerless, and Arjun found he could not locate any distance between the patient's words and his own interior. He sat with his face composed and his chest tight and afterwards sat alone in his car for twenty minutes. He is most afraid, he says, that the person he was before that hotel lobby is simply gone. What he is hoping for, more cautiously, is evidence that this is not true.
